papers.title: On the Seven-particle Clusters of Lennard-Jones and Thomson
papers.abstract: In this Letter, we develop a graph-geometric framework and prove that the pentagonal bipyramid (PBP) is the unique global minimiser of both the seven-particle Lennard-Jones energy in $\mathbb{R}^3$ and the seven-charge Thomson energy on $S^2$, up to rigid symmetries and particle relabelling. For the Thomson problem, this strengthens a recent deterministic global-optimality certificate to numerical tolerance into an exact global-optimality and uniqueness theorem. A weak-interaction graph, defined by thresholding pair geometry, organises configuration space without imposing symmetry or discarding any pair interaction. For Lennard-Jones, pair-energy counting, graph classification, subset bounds, and force balance reduce all possible minimisers to 29 bounded domains; exact geometric certificates exclude 28, localise the survivor near the PBP, and a uniform restoring-energy estimate proves uniqueness. The Thomson proof follows the same progression: graph reduction, geometric localisation, and rigidity, but finalises through whole-domain coercivity and a global localisation theorem. The same fivefold order therefore emerges in two very different physical settings: an unconstrained cluster with a preferred bond length and purely repelling charges confined to a sphere, showing a common geometric organising principle for seven particles that is not tied to either interaction.

papers.title: Spectroscopic method for determining the onset of clustering in supersonic gas jets
papers.abstract: This article presents an original spectroscopic method for determining the parameters of the initial stage of clustering in supersonic jets. The method was tested on supersonic jets of argon and nitrogen, excited by electrons at a distance of 30 millimetres from the nozzle exit, where the influence of secondary processes on the intensity of the observed radiation is significantly suppressed. For argon, the continuum emission from neutral excited clusters was used as an indicator of cluster formation in the supersonic argon jet. In the case of nitrogen, for which no emissions attributable exclusively to clusters have been recorded, a study was carried out on the effect of clustering on the redistribution of the intensities of atomic lines and molecular bands in the Lyman Birge Hopfield system.
